newsitem.title: UK: Dollar steady before U.S. trade report, G7 meeting.
newsitem.headline: Dollar steady before U.S. trade report, G7 meeting.

text.p: The dollar was little changed as the current preoccupation with U.S.-Japan trade relations led traders to look for direction to a U.S. trade report out later Thursday and the meeting of the Group of Seven starting Friday.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said overnight leaders from the G7 leading industrial nations will discuss the risk that further significant increases in Japan's trade surpluses will undermine growth in other countries and trigger a backlash against trade liberalisation.
His comments come after a report on Wednesday showed Japan's trade surplus with the U.S. and other countries surged in May.
Traders are now looking to the April U.S. trade report at 1230 GMT for confirmation that foreign exporters are getting more dollars to sell.

"The market doesn't look like it has done anything at all overnight but we've always got the chance of an extreme move if the trade numbers later today are out of line with expectations," said Austin White, the foreign exchange manager at Yamaichi Bank.
The dollar was quoted at 1.7310/15 marks at 0810 GMT from 1.7320/30 late Wednesday in Europe. It was at 113.40/50 yen from 113.41/46 yesterday.
Economists polled by Reuters expect the U.S. trade deficit widened to $10 billion in April from $8.5 billion in March.

Most traders are square going into the three-day G7 summit and the bilateral meeting between Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and U.S. President Bill Clinton later today. Analysts are, however, looking for the dollar to fall once the summit is out of the way.

"No-one wants to go short ahead of the G7 but given that Japan's trade surpluses will continue to rise in the next quarter or two, there will be downward pressure on dollar/yen," said Paul Megyessi, fx strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The dollar has more room for manoeuvre against other European currencies, traders said, with expectations of a broad-based European economic and monetary union seen supporting it in the weeks ahead.
"The long-term players are still looking to buy dollars against the Europeans on the weak euro argument," said Yamaichi's White.

Gains in dollar/mark will, however, be contingent on growth differentials between the U.S. and Germany being maintained. The dollar struggled to hold on to gains above 1.73 marks after the release of a stronger-than-expected Ifo survey in Germany.
The Ifo research institute said its West German business climate index rose to 95.3 in May from 94.7 in April while the region's business expectations index rose to 104.1 from 103.5.

"Germany continues to close the growth gap, which seems to justify some sort of pullback in dollar/mark," said Megyessi at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. He isn't looking for the dollar to fall below 1.72 marks anytime soon, though.

While the Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged in July, U.S. short rates still offer a 2.5 percentage point premium over their German counterparts. -Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 542 6284
